lines: Nothing about the incoming data changes at all, not one bit.
Just change the shape of the bucket you're pouring it into, and watch what happens.
Suddenly there's far more state sitting around, and two separate groups quietly become one.
A completeness claim needs something concrete to actually apply to.
That something is a chunk, a span carved out of the stream, holding whichever records belong to it.
This is the handful of real shapes that chunk is allowed to take.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Same incoming data, same chunk size, only the shape of the chunk changes.
Does changing just the shape cost anything extra to hold onto, or is a chunk a chunk?
answer: It costs plenty, and right away.
One shape hands each record to exactly one chunk. The other hands the same record to every chunk it happens to fall inside.
However many chunks a record lands in, that's how many copies of it now sit in memory.

lines: One shape never overlaps itself, so every record gets exactly one home.
The other shape overlaps on purpose, so a single record can end up living in several homes at once.
The more those homes overlap, the more copies of the same record are sitting around.
Here's a shape that isn't fixed at all, and can genuinely change its own mind later.
It just keeps stretching forward as long as something keeps showing up before it goes quiet too long.
Let something late slip in at just the right moment, and two of these that looked done quietly become one.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
Picture a chunk with no edges whatsoever, stretching across the entire stream from start to end.
Left on its own, with nothing extra told to it, does a chunk shaped like that ever actually say anything back?
answer: No, never, not on its own.
The usual rule for speaking up is simple: once a certain point in time has clearly passed, say something.
A chunk with no edge at all never reaches that point, so left alone it just stays silent forever.

lines: Left to that same old rule, a chunk shaped like this just sits there, silent, forever.
It isn't broken. It's simply waiting on a signal that was never going to arrive on its own.
Hand it a different, explicit signal instead, built just for it, and only then does it finally speak up.
Every chunk, for every single thing it's tracking, is quietly holding onto its own little pile of state.
That pile has to be thrown away eventually, the moment nothing new can possibly still belong to it.
Stop handing it anything new at all, and sooner or later, every single pile it was holding has to go.
Every number in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy model.
The extra cost that really showed up, and the two separate groups that really became one.
The silence that really never broke on its own, and the pile of state that really hit zero.
So: four very different shapes, each with its own idea of when it's actually done.
Overlap more, and you're quietly paying for it in however much state sits around.
And no matter the shape chosen, every single pile it was holding eventually has to go.
